content:
Some thoughts and open questions about TFT’s design, grouped by topic. Most of these come from playing at low Challenger (I was hovering around high Grandmaster when I last played), so they lean toward that end of the game.
Below is a quick prototype of one idea, followed by my working notes on TFT’s design. The notes are exploratory and not meant to be solid solutions; the prototype is what it looks like when I take one of them further.
Prototype: pool size indicator # A quick Unity mockup of one idea from these notes: showing how many copies of a champion are still available. Selecting a champion shows its remaining copies out of the total pool size, and the number updates live as units are rolled, bought, or adjusted. Hovering the number explains what it means for your shop.
Why show pool counts # Scouting the pool is an important skill to have in TFT, and showing pool counts would remove part of that skill expression. Scouting for items, positioning, and what people are building would still matter just as much, but counting copies would no longer separate experienced players from newer ones.
But as far as I know, the game never explains why you shouldn’t contest other players. Champion pools and pool sizes are core concepts that less involved players should understand, even if they don’t have a friend to explain it. Right now you learn it from a guide, a friend, or losing a lot. Some indicator of pool counts could help bridge this knowledge gap in a simple way.
Perfect knowledge of the pool might have its own issues. This is another very reasonable argument against this suggestion. If everyone knows exactly what’s left, everyone tends to make the same rational decisions, and lobbies get more uniform. Experienced players can already scout an approximate pool count though, so this extra knowledge is unlikely to make a big difference at a high level. So the question is whether streamlining the new player experience is worth narrowing that gap between experienced and inexperienced players. Put another way: is counting the pool a skill TFT should be testing?
My view is that while scouting is an important skill, it’s equally or more important for newer players to have something to point to when they can never seem to hit their units. Right now, many of them don’t even know the pool exists. Pool counts also better inform a player’s decision to pivot, which ties into the flexibility discussion below: if pivoting depends on reading the lobby correctly, pool counts make that read easier.
There are still many details to go through, ie: what exactly should count (copies in other players’ shops, in your own shop, on boards, on benches?). These matter for implementation, but the general idea comes first.
Design decisions # My first idea was an icon marking champions that are currently uncontested past a certain threshold. I dropped it for two reasons. Newer players might buy any unit with the icon on it, whether or not it fits their board. And the icon would pop in and out as players reroll and buy, which is visually jarring. There are a few other issues I found, but these two are really the main ones.
Instead, I decided to go with a ratio. A ratio is less jarring, but it still changes a lot, especially during players’ rolldowns. A number bouncing up and down draws the eye in a way that isn’t wanted, so in the real game it should probably update every second or few seconds rather than on every action. (The mockup updates instantly so the effect is easy to see.)
Finally, I ended up placing the ratio on a champion’s info card on the right. There’s a good argument against this: the info card shows information about that specific copy of a champion, while the pool count applies to every copy. I put it there anyway because the card already has a precedent for detailed numbers, and for tooltips you can hover to learn what they mean. Putting counts in the shop instead would mean five constantly changing numbers on screen, which feels like too much visual overload. There aren’t many other places for detailed champ info to show up.
Working notes # Everything below is my working notes: half-formed ideas, open questions, and things I’m still thinking through.
What do “flexible” and “creative” actually mean? # These words get thrown around all the time, but they’re really nebulous. Variety and monotony are much easier to define, so it might help to pin the fuzzier words to things that can actually be measured:
Flexibility: how predictable is a player’s final board from their early state? If you can call someone’s endgame comp from their opener or first augment, the game isn’t very flexible. And how do players who pivot place compared to players who stick to their line? Variety vs. monotony: how many distinct endgame boards show up in top 4, and how often does one player end up on the same endgame board across games? Creativity: maybe the feeling of making a choice the stats wouldn’t have recommended, and having it work. Hard to measure without just asking players. Line selection, theorycrafting, and endgame boards # At high levels, you usually pick a line and follow it. But I don’t think line selection itself is the problem. Your endgame board often gets locked in almost immediately, but the path there is probably the most creative and skill-expressive part of TFT: reading your opener, items, augments, and the lobby, and finding the right route through the midgame.
The problem is where those lines end up. Because stats are public, endgame boards are often the same handful of statistically strongest boards, so even after a creative midgame, the endgame can feel very monotonous. That’s why I think line selection/flexibility and theorycrafting are really closely related, maybe even the same problem: the path is creative, but the destination is mostly solved ahead of time.
Why flexibility matters # Flexibility is where a lot of skill expression comes from. If TFT were 100% rigid, players would just be waiting for the units they need to show up in their shop, which wouldn’t be very fun. The more flexible the game is, the more players can make use of any unit in their shop, and the more they can play around bad luck.
There’s a limit, though. If every unit were usable from every position, choosing units would feel meaningless, and the same problem would just show up with augments and items instead.
Committed vs. flexible players # From stage 2, almost every high-level player knows exactly what everyone else is going to play. Plans go wrong and people pivot in and out, but pivots are rare and generally avoided. There aren’t public stats on pivoting, but across my thousands of games at Grandmaster and Challenger, pivoting seems to be a rare occurrence, telling me most top players see it as negative EV. In the right spot, though, pivoting is the positive-EV play, and there aren’t specific enough stats to tell you when you’re in that spot. Pivoting there means going against the general consensus and trusting your own intuition, which is exactly why a successful pivot feels so good. I think moments like that are some of the most engaging in TFT.
But this makes me think line selection isn’t actually that bad. If pivoting became positive EV in general, a few things would go wrong. Pivots would feel less engaging, since they’d be the expected play instead of a creative idea that sidesteps the norms. Everyone would be pivoting unpredictably, making it nearly impossible to play around other players’ actions, so the game would feel more like a volatile stock market: chaotic and high variance. And it would be overwhelming for newer players, who’d have more to consider at more stages of the game. Optimally, some players should have a clearly defined gameplan, and other players should be able to play flexibly around them. The question is how much.
Right now it feels like 7 to 8 players (basically everyone) have their gameplan decided from the start. Maybe it should be closer to 6 or 7. That raises a few questions:
Should flexible players be on even footing with committed ones? Better? Worse? If flexible play is better on average, everyone ends up in a game of chicken, waiting for someone else to lock in first, and at high levels flexibility would simply always be the right choice. I think flexibility should be, at its core, a comeback mechanic: a way to turn a spot that would normally be bad into a decent one, not something that beats a committed line on its own. Basically, it should always be a solid plan B, but never plan A. What would move the ratio? The cost of changing direction (augment permanence, how permanent items are, how much value you lose selling), the reward for being uncontested (pool sizes, how much contesting hurts), and how much information players have (perfect scouting makes it easy to see who’s committed). When should players be forced into an endgame board? They obviously shouldn’t be switching boards every round. Pivoting should probably get more expensive as the game goes on, cheap early and costly late, with natural lock-in points around augments and the stage 4 rolldown. Since players are often already committed in stage 2, pivoting is already negative-EV by stage 3, which suggests that curve might be too steep too early. Why lines lock in early # Part of what narrows the destinations is how changeable each piece of your board is:
Champions are the most flexible. You can always roll for more. Items are mostly set. You usually can’t change your components or finished items, though there are a few ways to do it a limited number of times per game. This has become much less of a problem over time, with so many reforgers added in, alongside some augments and set mechanics (like charms). Augments are permanent. Once you have them, they’re there forever. Since augments are such a big part of your board’s strength and you can’t change them, your early augments narrow which endgame boards are realistically open to you. Additionally, switching later often means ending up weaker than the player who stuck to their line, since they chose more specific augments. Suboptimal items do the same thing. If you find a good direction early, the game gets very simple.
Set 8’s hero augments are the clearest example. Taking one meant you had to play that champion, or you’d lose the augment’s benefit entirely. That downside was so large that pivoting away was basically impossible, and adding lots of rerolls didn’t fix it. It created three problems (among others):
Taking the augment gave you one copy of the champion, but you usually still needed two more to upgrade it, even for “support” hero augments. If you didn’t hit them, you were stuck with a weak board. The reverse was true too: if you played around getting a specific hero augment and then weren’t offered it, your game fell apart just the same. If hitting the hero augment was too easy, everyone could force the best comp available. Some players liked being able to streamline a game around one champion, but not everyone wanted to do it every game. (Later sets improved on this by making some hero augments which were not guaranteed every game, but still in the pool.) It still happens in more modern sets. In Set 15, Deadlier Caps was technically a generic augment, but it was so much weaker on other lines that taking it all but locked you into Veigar, or, in a pinch, Lissandra, since Ziggs in a prismatic start lobby was nearly impossible without an econ start.
To a lesser degree, this is true of almost every augment. Most comps want some mix of items, econ, or combat augments, and all of those are shaped by choices made in stage 2, so your options narrow as the game goes on. The Ziggs case above shows this: Deadlier Caps is an item augment that should theoretically fit an AP carry like Ziggs, but because Ziggs needed an econ start, clicking an item augment in stage 2 made him too expensive to play. In a way, that’s normal and good: options narrowing as the game goes on is a healthy trait, and by the endgame players should have narrowed in on a comp. The problem is that the narrowing is too sharp. Being down even one augment is a huge liability for your final board, and that augment could be the very first one you pick in the game, if you don’t have a line selected by early stage 2.
One idea I’ve toyed with is making augments less set in stone, with some limited way to change them late in the game. To be clear, I don’t think it’s a good idea as it stands. It would be hard to implement, I haven’t thought it through, and it runs into a huge number of issues, for example:
Returning rewards only really works for combat augments. Augments that give gold or items can’t be taken back. On top of that, simply swapping these augments out is a terrible idea on paper. It makes early combat augments feel horrendous, since players who take them go most of the game with fewer resources than everyone else. It might make endgame boards even more similar, since everyone could steer toward the strongest board more easily. Those are just the first two problems that come to mind. Unless every one of them got solved out very thoroughly, I think it would create more problems than it fixes.
Theorycrafting and public stats # Playing creatively in the endgame at a high level doesn’t really exist anymore. I think it used to, but now endgame boards are more of a stats-mashing contest over who can combine the things with the best numbers, since all the numbers are already out there. It makes the end of the game feel closer to a trivia game than a teambuilding game.
With this many players, no one can out-theorycraft the whole community. The meta gets posted online, and nearly everyone ends up with the same meta knowledge, apart from the very top, where Challenger players rely on their own intuition or study groups to min-max.
There are still rare chances to get ahead of the curve. At the start of Set 15, I noticed in the first patch that T-Hex was overtuned, before other players did and before it got buffed even more. But moments like that are uncommon. Trait Tracker and Trait Ladder augments might have created more of them, but now there are tools that solve the optimal boards for those too.
A big part of the payoff of creativity is the feeling of discovery, of being a pioneer. That’s hard to get when so many eyes are on the same game and the community solves things so quickly. I don’t think that’s easily solvable in the modern climate.
The other side of this is that players need something to ground them. Not every player wants to theorycraft at all, especially new players, and they shouldn’t have to. Being able to see the meta without playing 500 games is really healthy for the playerbase as a whole. But, if everything is already known, creative players don’t get rewarded for their creativity. That’s most true at the highest level of play, where things are the most optimized. At lower levels, you can probably get away with a lot more.
I’m not sure what the answer is. Stats sites work because the same choice is worth approximately the same in every game, so it averages out. Choices whose value depends more on the specific game (the lobby, what others are playing, what’s left in the pool) would be harder to solve ahead of time, but they’d also add variance, making the game more luck-based and harder to learn. That’s probably not worth the tradeoff.
Some centralization is probably unavoidable. The meta will always settle around a few comps. The obvious way around that is, again, extremely high variance, but, as previously mentioned, then the game becomes a gamblefest in its own right, and having to theorycraft every single game would be too mentally taxing for most players.
So I don’t think the goal is to make theorycrafting the norm. Ideally, it would be rewarding, or even optimal, in a small minority of games, maybe 1 in 10 or 20. Right now, I can’t think of a reason not to play a meta comp in almost any game.
Related: when I took a few months off TFT, it wasn’t because games lacked variety. There’s already a ton of variation between games. It was more that I’d learned so much that even with that much variety, games started to feel like going through the motions. Every game eventually gets to that point for a dedicated player, and it’s a strength of TFT’s design that it took so long.
Positioning/Scouting # I question whether players should even have perfect information on enemy positioning. Even with random matchmaking, players can often narrow down who they’re likely to fight and reposition against them at the last second, which turns the end of each round into a twitch-reflex contest. I don’t think that should be part of the game. The catch is that players need to see enemy boards for other reasons: scouting champion counts, and clarity about what they’re fighting and losing against, which matters especially for newer players.
The idea I have in mind is that for the last 5 or so seconds of each planning phase, you only see a snapshot of each opponent’s board from that moment until the fight starts. The snapshot freezes everything, not just positions. A half-updating board would look strange and inconsistent, and it’s hard to change a comp much in 5 seconds anyway. You can still scout comps, items, and champion counts (including whether you’re contested), but you get almost no information on final positioning. Players can still reposition after the snapshot, so it becomes a game of prediction rather than reflexes.
The biggest issue is probably readability. Players need to clearly know when they’re looking at a snapshot instead of a live board, especially newer players and people watching streams or esports. That’s true of any way of hiding positioning, not just this one.
The other risk is how players might abuse the 5-second window. If there’s an advantage to doing as many actions as possible while your board can’t be seen, every top player will do it, and TFT gains a big APM check where you try to rush everything into the last 5 seconds. I’m not sure how much of an advantage hiding your actions actually is, though. Top players can already guess what others are doing from common rolling and leveling intervals, and items, augments, and current champions all carry over from the last turn, so it’s easy to see what direction a player is going. The main thing you gain from hiding your actions is positioning, which is exactly what the snapshot is meant to hide. Still, playtesting might show that hiding actions in those last 5 seconds matters much more than I think, and that top players would need good APM to compete.
TFT already has some APM checks, such as big rolldown turns, but those can be worked around, like by rolling earlier for a small loss of gold. I, myself, usually split my rolldown over two turns to make sure I stabilize my board in time. If the cost of not acting in the last 5 seconds is similarly small, it won’t affect top-level play much, and I think the snapshot is a worthwhile trade. If it turns out to be huge, it’s not worth adding such a punishing APM check to the game. There could also easily be more problems with it that I’m missing.
Matchmaking # Random matchmaking causes a lot of frustration. There are lobbies where two or three players are on long win or loss streaks and some players keep running into them while others don’t, and endgames where you fight the same strong player again every time someone is eliminated. In the long run this luck evens out, but in the short term it can feel incredibly bad to be on the wrong end of it.
One fix I considered would be to make matchmaking more uniform and predictable. I don’t mean literal round robin, just matchmaking where you can roughly tell who you’ll face and when. It might still feel unfair sometimes, but it would at least feel fairer, especially in the late game, where fight order can be a huge swing in placements.
The obvious problem is that if you knew exactly who you were fighting next, last-second repositioning against that player would become even stronger. With the snapshot from the positioning/scouting section, though, that problem mostly goes away.
Another issue is that counting turns and memorizing your next few opponents becomes a new skill top-level players would have to learn, and it’s ultimately not a skill I think TFT should be testing. That said, I think that even with this problem, predictable matchmaking was still worth consideration.
The biggest problem, and the reason I ultimately rejected this idea myself, is the existence of loss-streak traits. Right now, selling your board against a loss streaker is a questionable decision. Early on you usually only have about a 30% chance to fight them, and selling removes any chance of winning a fight until your next spike. However, if you knew you were fighting them, you’d sell your board nearly every time. Loss-streak traits are a fan favorite, likely because of how high variance they are, and predictable matchmaking would practically remove all possibility of them returning.
So I don’t think predictable matchmaking is worth it, at least early on.
summary: A Unity prototype of a champion pool indicator, plus working notes on Teamfight Tactics’ design from a Grandmaster to Challenger player: flexibility, public stats, matchmaking, and more.
title: Thoughts on TFT's Design

content:
Link to Game # https://suareal.itch.io/websters
Team Size/Time constraint # Main programmer and designer in a team of 2. Made in 2 days for a game jam. What I did # Came up with the core concept and designed the full game loop Programmed the vast majority of the game, including: Online multiplayer with FishNet, keeping every player’s state, turns, and submissions in sync Round flow through the prompt, define, decoy, and guess phases Building each round’s word bank from players’ prompt answers plus 10 random dictionary words The definition builder, which restricts the definer to words from the bank Decoy submission, shuffling decoys in with the real word, and guess handling Game Overview # Websters is a Jackbox-style party game about defining a word with completely unrelated words, leading to nonsensical definitions, and a lot of questioning of your friends’ intelligence. Gameplay Loop # Prompt: Every player answers a prompt. Their answers become the shared word bank for the round. Define: One player picks a secret word and has to describe it using only words from the bank. Ten random dictionary words are thrown in too, to help fill in gaps. Decoy: Everyone else reads the description they wrote and writes a decoy/fake word they think fits it. Guess: All the decoys are revealed alongside the real word, and everyone tries to pick out the real one. For example, if my prompt answer was “I really enjoy eating pancakes” and my secret word is cannibal, I have to describe a cannibal with “I, really, enjoy, eating, pancakes,” plus whatever everyone else wrote and the random words.
summary: A Jackbox-style party game where you define a word using only everyone elses words
title: Websters

content:
Link to Game # https://charliedreemur.itch.io/holoswipe
Team Size/Time constraint # Worked as a programmer and designer in a team of 4, for a 2 week long Game Jam. What I did # Wrote initial game concept summary Programmed disasters, loot drops, player stats, UI, and Sound Designed and balanced player stats, items, and disasters Game Overview # Holoswipe is a fast-paced 3d roguelike where the objective is to survive one week as an obsessed Hololive Fan. Each day you must buy run around booths to collect coins and buy enough merch to prove your allegiance. Merch items give you stats in return which can increase your income, discount items, or help you avoid money-stealing disasters. Gameplay Design # The goal of the game is to get enough fan score each day to reach the next day. This is similar to games like balatro, where the only objective is to get your score high enough to win.
Money: Players obtain money in 2 ways, through coins which spawn randomly and frequently around the map and salary, a flat sum of money which is
Items: Items will spawn in set areas in the map, and can be bought with money. With some exceptions, item spawns will always be random, though the location they spawn is the same each time. Items are the core of the gameplay, and the only way for players to increase their stats and fanscore enough to reach the target. The goal of random item spawns is to offer a different experience/item build for multiple playthroughs.
Limited inventory: Players have a limited space to hold items, and players can organize their inventory to hold more. This allows for a slight optimization minigame, as well as providing for more item balancing levers (items that are cheaper are stronger earlier on when inventory space isn’t an issue, whereas items that take up less space are more useful later when the player has a strong economy built). Additionally, it’s simply cool to see the item sprites in your inventory.
Disasters: Disasters are thematic events which can impede the player’s movement, or steal their money. These are mainly intended to keep players on their toes and moving all the time, increasing tension, as well as providing homage to Hololive members.
Loot spawns: Loot spawns are the counterpart to disasters. Since the player can simply leave the convention early if they want, these loot spawns incentivize the player to stay in the convention for as long as they can, as well as providing exciting moments where players can be dropped expensive items.
Time limit: Each day, there is a time limit before the player will be chased out by enemies which get increasingly faster and deduct a large sum of money if they reach. The idea behind these enemies is to allow a slight bit of leeway to the player, as well as letting players to feel how much “stronger” they are later in the game. Since the enemies slowly scale up their speed, high speed builds will be able to run from them for longer, and create fun moments.
Item Balance # Overall philosophy: While testing, I found that there were numerous times where the best strategy was simply amassing a large sum of fan score through items (As opposed to other items which offer other stats in addition such as luck, movespeed, or discount). While optimal, it felt terrible, as the items the player would buy would keep them at near base stats throughout the entire playthrough, resulting in them feeling the same at the end of the game as they do at the start. Because of this, a lot of the stat allocation and balancing is intended to incentivize players to get a wide variety of stats so they feel much stronger by the end, almost as though they’re cheating compared to the start. Most viable builds will include comically high speed, enough luck to make it rain loot, or so much discount that items are practically free, allowing for a satisfying sense of progression.
Posters and pins: special items which give increased stats based on the other items in your inventory. These are the cruxes of our archetypes, and powerful items which players should feel happy to build around.
Plushies: Items which always spawn in the same location and give pure fanscore. These are intentionally extremely understatted for 2 reasons: The fact that these always spawn means that they would reduce variation and replayability. Additionally, since they don’t give any stat other than fanscore, they don’t make the player feel any stronger. However, they are useful later on, as they take up very little space, and players who have an excess of money can buy them to fill in their empty inventory slots efficiently.
summary: A fast paced shopping spree roguelike created for HoloJam 6

Your browser does not support the video tag. Team Size/Time constraint # Worked as the lead of design in a team of 9, starting in Oct 2024, currently ongoing. What I did # Lead all design decisions, working in several design disciplines such as Mechanics, Technical, UX, QA etc. Authored 20+ design documents, including Gameplay Loops, Feature Breakdowns, Asset Lists, etc. Worked in Unreal Engine using Blueprint and C++ to implement and balance level designs Game Overview # In Master Dancer, you meet the famous dancer Loïe Fuller, the first to integrate technology into modern dance. As a player, you engage in action games to learn her movement principles and, guided by Virtual Loïe, explore her world. You will use modern VR technology to create your own unique dance, becoming a Master Dancer yourself! Star Maker # Star maker is one of the minigames meant to teach players dance principles. In this game, players must hit orbs flying at them towards targets in time with the music. The core design pillars of Star Maker are to teach players to do strong, direct movements, have players feel in tune with the music, and to be very forgiving in gameplay.
Notable Features # Designed an orb trajectory prediction system so that the orb hits targets when it appears to from the player’s perspective. Designed an aim assist feature to make game feel more satisfying. The strength is linearly curved so that wildly inaccurate hit will still be very off, while closer hits will hit the target. Adjusted aim assist strength through multiple playtest sessions. Designed a music looping system in order to give players multiple tries, reducing frustrayion while maintaining the musicality of the game. Music Roundabout # Music Roundabout (called Music Game while in development) is another minigame meant to teach players dance principles. In this game, players will activate orbs which rotate around them, creating a melody. The core design pillars of Music Roundabout are to teach players twisting motion, as well as a light tapping motion. In addition, players should feel as though they are creating music as they play.
Notable Features # Designed an orb charging system where players had to follow the rotating orb with their hand to incentivize players to twist their hips naturally. Designed visual indicators for players to know when to activate orbs, even with no sound (Although, sound was of course vital for this minigame). Chose to limit the arc of the orb, from traversing in a full circle to a half circle, to prevent players from getting dizzy and tangled in the VR headset’s wire.
